title: Sharing the Value of AI training
content:
Today we publish Sharing the value of AI training: a collective remuneration mechanism, a discussion paper and our contribution to the European Commission’s targeted consultation on a better copyright environment for European creativity and innovation.

The paper builds on Beyond AI and Copyright, which we published in June 2025, and follows the call for a European content levy that Mistral made earlier this year. It sets out, as a basis for discussion, a more detailed mechanism tied to the training of AI models and built with the instruments of EU copyright and market-access law.

In its call for evidence, the Commission states that it wants to “improve the conditions for creators’ remuneration, while making it easier for providers of generative AI to access copyright-protected content”. These objectives pull in different directions. Measures aimed at one tend to come at the cost of the other: stricter reservation regimes make access to data for AI development harder, while broader exceptions leave rightholders without remuneration.

title: The Cloud and AI Development Act Proposal
content:
Throughout the EU, there is a clear political ambition to use public procurement as a lever to reduce reliance on a small number of non-EU cloud service providers and to open the market to a wider range of providers. The Commission presents its proposal for a Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) as a way to ‘decrease overreliance on certain providers’. Yet, as the CADA proposal is designed, it is more likely to preserve the status quo than to enable public procurement to be used to scale up an open source and interoperable European digital stack.

In this report, Zuzanna Warso and Kristina Irion, an Associate Professor at the Institute for Information Law, University of Amsterdam, examine Title IV of the CADA proposal entitled ‘Autonomy’, which covers a cloud computing sovereignty framework with its four Union assurance levels, and risk assessments and public procurement of cloud computing services used by public sector bodies in the Member States and Union entities.

title: Digital Commons Policy Summit 2026
content:
On 12 November, the NGI Commons Initiative is organising the Digital Commons Policy Summit 2026 in Brussels. Building on the previous year’s edition, this year’s summit will focus on ‘Digital commons and the Open Internet Stack for a competitive Europe’. The summit’s goal is to advance and discuss strategies to achieve European digital sovereignty and to ensure that Digital Commons have a role in the new European Open Internet Stack.

The gathering will bring together policymakers, regulators, funders and practitioners to discuss tech sovereignty and open source.

As part of the NGI Commons consortium, Open Future will lead session 2, which will be moderated by Paul Keller (Director of Policy) and titled ‘The Digital Commons Strategic Agenda’. Confirmed speakers include Jan Penfrat (EDRi, Senior Policy Advisor), Plixavra Vogiatzoglou (University of Amsterdam Institute for Information Law (IViR)), and Laszlo Igneczi (Executive Director of OpenForum Europe).

Our Director of Research, Zuzanna Warso, will also speak at the summit to discuss the Tech Sovereignty Package and the Digital Commons.

title: From a Registry to a Registry Ecosystem
content:
Today, we publish a new strategy paper on how Europe’s emerging copyright infrastructure should be developed. Authored by Paul Keller and Sebastian Posth – and developed as part of the CommonsDB pilot – the paper distils 18 months of building and operating a working public registry of the public domain into a proposal for how a system of copyright registries should be organised and the role that public institutions should play in it.

For most of its history, European copyright law has functioned without formal registration. Protection arises automatically, and there is no public record of what is protected, by whom, or under what conditions. This was appropriate for as long as copyright governed a slow-moving world of professional intermediaries. But automated systems now make decisions relevant to copyright about billions of works, such as filtering uploads, assembling training data for artificial intelligence, and resolving reuse permissions. Those systems depend on reliable, machine-readable rights information. But currently there is no public infrastructure that can provide it at scale.

title: Open Future’s response to the Call for Evidence on the AI Strategy for the Cultural and Creative Sectors
content:
Open Future has submitted a response to the European Commission’s call for evidence on the Artificial intelligence strategy for the cultural and creative sectors.

The call frames the role of these sectors as adopters of AI and providers of data. Our response argues that this definition is too narrow and proposes an additional role: the development and governance of public data infrastructure to make cultural data accessible to Europe’s public AI ecosystem. We refer to this as cultural sovereignty: as cultural resources are converted into proprietary data by non-European providers, Europe requires institutions that can maintain open, publicly governed infrastructure in the public interest.

This submission is based on our contribution to the Europeana Initiative’s Public AI white paper and supports Europeana’s own response to the Call for Evidence. Our feasibility study for a European Books Data Commons illustrates how this approach could be applied to one category of material: a shared, library-governed layer that makes millions of digitised public-domain books AI-ready on infrastructure controlled by the contributing institutions.

title: The shaky sovereignty bet behind the EU’s AI Gigafactories
content:
In her  State of the Union address in September 2025, Ursula von der Leyen identified AI Gigafactories (AIGF) as one of the centrepieces of Europe’s technological sovereignty agenda.  In that speech, the president of the European Commission said:

A European AI is essential for our future independence. It will help power our industries and our societies (…). We are massively investing in European AI Gigafactories. They support our innovative start-ups to develop, train, and deploy their next-generation AI models. When we called on the private sector to join forces with us, the response was overwhelming.

A European AI is essential for our future independence. It will help power our industries and our societies (…). We are massively investing in European AI Gigafactories. They support our innovative start-ups to develop, train, and deploy their next-generation AI models. When we called on the private sector to join forces with us, the response was overwhelming.

With this year’s State of the Union approaching, it is worth asking how that agenda has unfolded over the past year.

title: Launch of Mosaic: a mission for the knowledge commons in the age of AI
content:
Wikimania 2026 took place in Paris in July, marking the 25th Anniversary of Wikipedia. One of the key themes addressed at the conference was the impact of AI technologies on Wikimedia and how they can be used to support free knowledge.

We took this opportunity to launch our new white paper, published in collaboration with Wikimedia Switzerland and titled Wikimedia, the commons, and the new AI knowledge loop. A mission for 2030. We also organized two connected events in partnership with the AI-BRIDGES initiative: an invitation-only roundtable and a public session at the conference. These events aimed to launch Mosaic, a consortium of organizations that steward the knowledge commons and build public AI solutions. Mosaic will support the mission outlined in the white paper.The Mosaic mission is carried out by a consortium of organisations that manage the knowledge commons and develop public AI solutions.

title: Workshop on Policies for the Knowledge Commons
content:
On 22 July, Open Future partnered with Inria to host a workshop at Inria’s Paris offices, exploring a shared EU policy agenda for the knowledge commons. The workshop took place against the backdrop of the European Commission’s consultation around an Open Digital Ecosystem Strategy and the subsequent Tech Sovereignty Package. These initiatives have shaped recent discussions on digital sovereignty.

The session brought together representatives from commons projects, such as Wikipedia and Software Heritage; research institutions including CNRS; organizations such as OpenMined, along with policymakers and allied stakeholders.The workshop addressed a gap in the current EU digital sovereignty debate. While policy attention has focused heavily on open-source software, knowledge commons projects, such as Wikipedia and OpenStreetMap, which are foundational layers of the knowledge infrastructure relied on by both human understanding and AI systems, remain underrepresented. These projects face unique challenges regarding sustainability, licensing, and reciprocity that existing policy frameworks do not adequately address.

title: CommonsDB Final Conference
content: Whether a work can be freely reused ought to be a simple question to answer. In practice it rarely is. Information about copyright status—whether something is in the public domain, or available under an open license—is scattered across catalogs, collection pages and terms-of-use notices, is frequently incomplete, and is almost never machine-readable. Works that are free to use are hard to find, and harder still to reuse with confidence. The digital commons is vast, but largely invisible to the systems that would put it to work.

title: The EU has launched a call for tenders for AI Gigafactories
content:
The European Commission has launched a call for tenders to establish up to seven AI Gigafactories across the EU: four medium-scale sites with at least 75,000 advanced AI accelerators each and three large-scale sites with at least 100,000. According to the tender specifications, the AIGF initiative aims to strengthen the EU’s sovereignty and competitiveness and serve as a “catalyst for the evolution of a resilient European AI ecosystem.”

The headline figure for the investment is €30 billion. Currently, the only firm EU commitment is around €1 billion, and member states are expected to match this amount. Any additional EU funding will depend on the next MFF. Industry partners will cover the vast majority of the project. The public contribution will come in the form of a guarantee to purchase computing access time.

Applications close on 12 November 2026. Award decisions are expected in early 2027, with construction set to begin the same year. Of the EU’s public share, only around €1 billion is currently secured; the rest depends on the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), which member states have yet to agree on.
